topicClassValue: The alimentary canal of the lepidopteran caterpillar is distinct from other insects for being strongly alkaline, which is also the case for the silkworm, Bombyx mori gut. To understand whether silkworms harbor active gut microbes that interact with the host, we investigated the bacterial community of the silkworm larval gut. We found several bacterial species, including Sphingomonas paucimobilis, Acinetobacter guillouiae, and Methylobacterium populi, with a relatively high percentage in active feeding larval stages. The bioassay revealed that Sphingomonas paucimobilis (strain ZJ1) inoculated larvae had a higher survival rate and body weight against the toxic plant secondary metabolite flavonoid Kaempferol-3-O-glucosyl rutinoside (K3GR). Furthermore, we identified an alkaline-resistant β-glucosidase from ZJ1, which effectively degraded K3GR into K3R with low toxicity. These results suggest that lepidopteran gut microbiota can also help host degrade toxic substances even in the extremely alkaline gut environment. Using silkworm gut microbiota as an experimental system, our study not only provides the first experimental evidence to support that gut bacteria affect lepidopteran host biology by detoxification, but also deepens our understanding of the vast range of interactions between insects and microbes.
